title: The Black Crane
subtitle: San Francisco, Eight Nights in the Fog of November 1938

listing.title: The Black Crane 🪶
listing.blurb: San Francisco, November 1938: your partner is shot dead in an alley off Jackson Street on the first night of a job for a client with three names, and everyone in town wants a black-lacquered crane coming in from Lisbon on a rusty freighter. A courteous fat collector, a frightened gunsel, a widow whose story changes every time you ask, and a homicide lieutenant who has given you until Armistice Day before he arrests you for it. Levels 3–7.

synopsis: San Francisco in November 1938 is a city that has just built two of the longest bridges in the world and is filling in a shoal in the middle of the Bay to hold a World's Fair. The Bay Bridge is two years old, the Golden Gate eighteen months; out past Yerba Buena Island, on four hundred acres of dredged mud now called Treasure Island, carpenters and plasterers are racing to finish the Golden Gate International Exposition by February. The fog comes in every evening through the Gate like a tide. On Thursday 3 November a young woman in a good grey coat with a silver fox collar walks into the office of Corrigan & Delaney, Confidential Inquiries, on the sixth floor of the Monadnock Building on Market Street, gives her name as Mrs. Helen Strand, and pays two hundred dollars to have the agency 'take possession of a family heirloom' before anybody else does: a black-lacquered crane statuette, fourteen inches high, coming in from Lisbon aboard the Portuguese freighter Serra da Estrela. By eleven that night the agency's founding partner, Ned Corrigan, is lying dead in Tallow Alley, a cobbled lane off Jackson Street on the edge of Chinatown, shot twice with a .32, his own revolver still in its holster. By morning the client has checked out of her hotel under a second name, and Lieutenant Frank Dolan of Homicide, who learned the trade from Ned and loved him, has noted that the agency's partners collect five thousand dollars of insurance on Ned's death. He gives them until Armistice Day. Over eight days and nights the party must find out who their client really is, meet the freighter in the fog on the Embarcadero, sit in on an auction that ends in a Tommy gun and a car chase across the Bay Bridge to the half-built Exposition, and finally stand in a penthouse on top of Nob Hill with every person who wants the crane, and the person who killed Ned Corrigan, in the same room. Everyone has a story about what is under the lacquer. Almost all of them are wrong.
hook: Friday 4 November 1938, a quarter past one in the morning. The telephone in the dark goes and keeps going. It is Lieutenant Frank Dolan of Homicide, and his voice is flat in the way a man's voice goes flat when he is holding something heavy. 'It's Ned,' he says. 'Tallow Alley, off Jackson by the old Marsh warehouse. Come down. Come down now, and don't touch anything, and Delaney, don't bring a gun.' The fog is in so thick on Kearny Street that the streetlamps are only yellow smudges. There are two prowl cars at the mouth of the alley with their spotlights on, and in the middle of the wet cobbles, under a coat somebody has laid over him, is the man who taught every one of you something. Ned's hat has rolled against the warehouse wall. His hand is still in his coat pocket, where he kept his cigarettes. Ten hours ago he took two hundred dollars from a pretty woman with a foreign accent and said, 'Easiest money we'll see all year.'

setting.name: San Francisco, Thursday 3 to Saturday 12 November 1938
setting.description: The real San Francisco of late 1938, with fictional people moving through it. A city of hills and fog and seven hundred thousand people on the tip of a peninsula, rebuilt after 1906 and proud of it. Market Street runs like a spine from the Ferry Building, where fifty thousand commuters a day still come off the ferries from Oakland and Marin even though the Bay Bridge is open; the Key System trains rumble across the lower deck of the bridge into the new Terminal at First and Mission. The cable cars climb Nob Hill past the Fairmont and the Mark Hopkins, where the penthouse on the nineteenth floor is being talked about as a cocktail lounge for next year. Below them Chinatown is a crowded, busy neighbourhood of families, shops, schools, family associations and churches, with a telephone exchange on Washington Street whose operators know every subscriber by name; it borders the old Barbary Coast and the brick warehouses of Jackson Square, where import firms keep their offices, and the Hall of Justice on Kearny Street, which faces Portsmouth Square and holds the police, the courts, the city jail and the morgue under one roof. North Beach is Italian and noisy and smells of coffee; the Fillmore and Japantown are a streetcar ride west; Russian Hill has the steep stairs and the views. Along the Embarcadero the piers are numbered odd to the north of the Ferry Building and even to the south; four years after the waterfront strike of 1934 the longshoremen have their hiring hall, the shipowners have their grievances, and a few men like Mick Larrabee still run their piers as private kingdoms. Out in the Bay, on Treasure Island, the Exposition is going up: the Tower of the Sun, the Court of the Moon, great plaster pavilions with no roofs yet, floodlit at night so the crews can work, joined to Yerba Buena Island and the bridge by a causeway. Europe is a long way off, but not as far as it was: the evening papers are full of Munich, of refugees in Lisbon and Marseille, and on the night of 10 November, of the burning of synagogues across Germany and Austria.
setting.atmosphere: Fog, foghorns, and wet cobbles. The bell of a cable car on a hill you cannot see. Neon smeared on a rain-slick sidewalk, a radio playing in a cigar store, a newsboy shouting the late final, the smell of roasting coffee on Columbus Avenue and of tar and fish oil on the Embarcadero. This is a hard-boiled paperback, not a pageant: people lie for reasons, mostly bad and sometimes good, and the players should feel that every conversation is a trade. Violence is quick, loud and costly: a gunshot downtown brings the prowl cars in two minutes and a headline in the morning. Competence is the fantasy: the right question to a cable-car gripman, the bribe that is exactly the right size, the detail on a dead man's sleeve. Ground scenes in 1938: nickel phone calls, Philco radios, Lucky Strikes and Chesterfields, fedoras and gabardine, Packards and Ford V8s, the Chronicle and the Examiner, a Western Union boy on a bicycle, a cup of coffee for a nickel and a steak dinner for a dollar. There are no portable radios, no police radios in most cars beyond a receiver, no fingerprint file you can search in a day. Information lives in people's heads, in paper, and in the fog.

regions.name: Downtown and Market Street
regions.description: The Monadnock Building at 681 Market, where Corrigan & Delaney rent two rooms on the sixth floor with frosted glass doors and a radiator that knocks; the Palace Hotel across the street; the Sir Francis Drake and the St. Francis on Union Square; the Western Union main office; the Matson Line ticket office; Montgomery Street's banks and bond houses, the 'Wall Street of the West'; Sutter Street's galleries and auction rooms, including Gilchrist & Lowe.

regions.name: Chinatown, Jackson Square and the Hall of Justice
regions.description: Grant Avenue and its side streets: grocers, herbalists, a Chinese-language daily, the Chinatown Telephone Exchange on Washington Street in its pagoda-roofed building, family association halls, Old St. Mary's at the corner of California. To the east, across Kearny, Portsmouth Square and the grey bulk of the Hall of Justice; past it, the brick warehouses of Jackson Square, and Tallow Alley, a dead-end lane of loading doors where Marsh Pacific Trading keeps a shuttered warehouse. The people here are residents, workers and families like anywhere else in the city, and some of them saw something on Thursday night.

regions.name: Nob Hill and Russian Hill
regions.description: Nob Hill is money: the Fairmont and the Mark Hopkins facing each other across California Street, Grace Cathedral half built, the Pacific Union Club in the old Flood mansion, and the California Street cable cars grinding up from Kearny. The Mark Hopkins' nineteenth-floor penthouse is let to Mr. Ambrose Pellingham for the season. Russian Hill, a few steep blocks north, is where Corinne Marsh lives in a shingled house on Vallejo Street with a view of Alcatraz and a mortgage she cannot pay.

regions.name: The Embarcadero
regions.description: Three miles of piers, sheds and rail spurs along the waterfront from Fisherman's Wharf to China Basin, under the new bridge. Pier 32, south of the Ferry Building, is Larrabee's: his stevedoring outfit works it, his men drink at the Anchor Grill across the Belt Line tracks, and his office looks over the berth where the Serra da Estrela will tie up. The U.S. Appraiser's Stores on Sansome and Washington is where Customs examines anything that comes in with a value.

regions.name: The Bay Bridge and Treasure Island
regions.description: The San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge, upper deck for automobiles, lower deck for trucks and the interurban trains, tunnelling through Yerba Buena Island halfway across. Below the island, a causeway runs out to Treasure Island, where the Exposition's pavilions stand in plaster and scaffolding under floodlights, the Tower of the Sun rises four hundred feet over half-planted gardens, and Larrabee's trucks haul fill and timber on night contracts. At night it is a ghost city of lights, mud and watchmen.

campaignRules.name: Heat
campaignRules.description: San Francisco has a single Heat score for the party, 0 to 10, which the GM tracks openly in the world state and announces every time it changes. It starts at 2, because Dolan already suspects the agency. It rises: +1 for being seen somewhere you should not be (a crime scene, a locked warehouse, a dead man's house); +1 for leaning hard on someone with friends (Larrabee's men, a Nob Hill matron, a customs officer); +2 for a gunshot fired downtown; +2 for a body; +3 for a gunfight or car chase the police see; +1 for each lie to Dolan he later catches. It falls by 1 for each full day the party spends quiet, and by 2 if they bring Dolan something true and useful. At 3 Dolan has the party tailed and calls them in to the Hall of Justice whenever he likes. At 6 Larrabee is told to 'take care of' the party and Dolan moves Cass Delaney's arrest forward by a day. At 9 the city is closed: the agency's license is suspended, Dolan has warrants, and the hotels and garages the party relies on will not have them.

campaignRules.name: The Three-Clue Rule
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the players must reach has at least three clues, in three different places, listed in each scenario and in the control file. Core clues are found automatically by any character who looks in the right place and uses a sensible skill (Forensics on a body, Research at the Hall of Records, Insight on a liar): no roll. Rolls add detail, speed, or a bonus clue; a failed roll costs time, Heat or goodwill, never the case. If the players are stuck, use the Case Board (below) rather than inventing a new clue in a convenient place, and never move the killer.

campaignRules.name: The Case Board
campaignRules.description: At the start of each session, or whenever the table stalls for more than a few minutes, the GM sums up what the agency knows as if pinned to the corkboard in Ned's office: the suspects, with what each wants and the last thing they lied about; the open questions; and two or three leads not yet followed, each with a place to go. The board is honest: it lists what the characters know, not what the GM knows, and it reminds players of clues they found and forgot. Dot Farrell, the agency's secretary, keeps the real one, and players can ask her what is on it.

campaignRules.name: Armistice Day
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a fixed calendar the GM tracks in the world state. Dolan gives the party until midnight on Friday 11 November, Armistice Day, and then he arrests Cass Delaney for Ned's murder (at Heat 6, Thursday 10 November). Fixed events: Monday 7 November, the Serra da Estrela arrives through the Gate at dusk; Tuesday 8, Election Day, Customs releases the crate; Wednesday 9, the auction is announced; Thursday 10, the evening papers carry news of the pogrom in Germany and Austria, and the auction at Gilchrist & Lowe is held at eight; Friday 11, the parade on Market Street at eleven, and Mr. Pellingham's party in the penthouse at ten that night; Saturday 12, at nine in the morning, the Matson liner sails for Honolulu from Pier 35. Each day has about five useful scenes. Time should feel short.

campaignRules.name: Money, Bribes and Favors
campaignRules.description: Each character's money is the 'Wallet containing $NN' line on their sheet. 1938 prices: a cup of coffee 5 cents, a payphone call a nickel, a cab across downtown 50 cents, a steak dinner $1, a room at a decent hotel $3 a night and at the Mark Hopkins $15, a fifth of rye $1.50, a box of .38 shells $1.25. Bribes: a doorman or bellhop $1, a hotel desk clerk $5, a desk sergeant $10, a longshore gang boss $20, a copy of a coroner's report $50, a customs inspector who forgets a crate $100 and a long memory. Favors are tracked by name; anyone who does the party a favor will one day ask for one back, and the GM should remember to collect.

explorationRules: This is a city campaign and the map is a schematic of San Francisco's northeast corner, from Russian Hill to the piers, with Treasure Island out in the Bay. Within the city the unit of time is the scene (roughly an hour or two), and travel is quick but never free: a cab costs fifty cents and a driver who remembers you, a cable car costs a nickel and a gripman who remembers you, walking up Nob Hill costs ten minutes and your breath. Run each scenario as a small sandbox of named places, with the other players in the game (Pellingham, Corinne Marsh, Larrabee, Dolan, the client) acting on their own clocks and on what they know. Nobody is omniscient: Larrabee knows what Sergeant Kerrigan tells him, Pellingham what Lonnie sees, Corinne what she overhears and what she reads in the papers. Clues are physical and human: a hair on a sleeve, an entry in a register, a cloakroom girl's memory. Skill checks are stated with a DC and a failure outcome; failures cost time, Heat or position, and never close a lead for good. Let the city breathe between scenes: the foghorns at Point Bonita and Alcatraz, a Filipino dance hall on Kearny with a ten-cent-a-dance band, a North Beach bakery at four in the morning, a ferry sliding into the Ferry Building slip, the Exposition's floodlights out in the Bay like a city on another planet. The players should come away knowing what San Francisco felt like in the last autumn before the war.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. All characters are fictional; the backdrop (the Bay Bridge, the Exposition under construction on Treasure Island, the California Street cable cars, the Chinatown Telephone Exchange, the Hall of Justice, the 1938 refugee crisis, the 8 November election and the November pogrom in Germany and Austria) is real. No real private person appears. Real public figures stay off-stage and unnamed. No plot, name or scene is taken from any existing novel or film.
controlFile.theKiller: Corinne Marsh, 42, widow of the importer Carlton Marsh, shot Ned Corrigan twice with her late husband's Colt .32 pocket pistol at about 11:05 pm on Thursday 3 November, at the loading door of Marsh Pacific's warehouse in Tallow Alley. She was at the Community Chest ball at the Fairmont that night in a grey gown and a silver fox stole, and thirty people will swear she was there. She slipped out by the Mason Street side door at 10:42, rode the California Street cable car down to Kearny, walked four blocks north past the Hall of Justice, met Ned, shot him when he turned to light her cigarette, dropped the pistol into an ash can at the mouth of the alley as she ran, and rode a cable car back up the hill. She was in the ladies' lounge by 11:35, threw her scorched gloves in the wastebasket, put on the spare pair in her evening bag, and was dancing by 11:45. Why: Ned had telephoned her that evening. He had learned from his client that the crane in her late husband's shipment held a refugee family's savings, and he offered her an honest deal: a five-thousand-dollar finder's fee from the family if she released the crate without a fight. Corinne, who is three months from losing her house and has nothing but Carlton's debts, understood that Ned could prove the money was not hers, and that anyone who knew it would never stop knowing it. She chose the alley because it was hers, and dark. She is not a monster and not a femme fatale: she is a former nightclub singer who married up, was frightened of being poor again all her life, and made one irrevocable decision in four minutes. She has been making the next one, and the next, ever since.
controlFile.theCrane: The Black Crane is a genuine late-seventeenth-century Japanese lacquer figure: a red-crowned crane standing on one leg on a rock, carved in hinoki cypress, fourteen inches high, in black urushi lacquer with a vermilion crown and a faint gold maki-e ripple on the base. It belonged for forty years to the collection of Dr. Otto Ehrlich, a Viennese physician, who carried it out of Austria in May 1938, after the Anschluss, as the one valuable thing he could get past the border. It is worth about $12,000 to the right buyer. In Lisbon, where the Ehrlichs are waiting for American immigration visas, a restorer opened the hollow base and sealed inside it a roll of United States Treasury bearer bonds worth $38,000, which Otto bought through a Zurich bank in 1934 when he saw what was coming, and which the Portuguese police would have confiscated at the first search. Carlton Marsh, an American importer of cork and wine whom the Ehrlichs met at a pension, offered to ship the crane to San Francisco as Marsh Pacific merchandise and deposit the bonds in a San Francisco bank in Magda Ehrlich's name, so that the family could show the American consul proof of funds. Carlton was a gambler and a debtor but, this once, an honest man. He died of a heart attack on the steps of the Alfama on 19 August 1938, two days after the crane was loaded. Nothing in the crane is a jewel, a relic or a secret formula. What is under the lacquer is cypress wood. What is in the base is a family's way out.
whoWantsItAndWhy: Magda Ehrlich, 27, the client, who has used three names (Mrs. Helen Strand to the agency, Miss Marta Lind at the Sir Francis Drake, and her own). She came ahead on a sixty-day visitor's visa to collect the bonds. The family's visa interview at the American consulate in Lisbon is Monday 21 November; a San Francisco bank must cable proof of funds by Friday 18 November, or the visas are refused and the Portuguese will not renew their transit permits. Legally the crate belongs to Marsh Pacific, and a lawyer told her probate would take a year, so she asked Ned to help her take it. She lies because every official she has met since March has been a danger to her, and because her passport now carries the red 'J' stamp the Reich began adding in October. She did not kill Ned. At 11:02 pm she was at the Western Union office on Market Street cabling her father; the cable is time-stamped.

Ambrose Pellingham, 58, a Philadelphia coal heir and collector of Japanese lacquer who winters in Lisbon and buys the heirlooms of refugees at a tenth of their worth, courteously and legally. He tried to buy the crane from Otto Ehrlich in July for $800 and was refused. He does not know about the bonds and would not much care; he wants the crane, which he believes (correctly) is the finest piece of its kind outside Japan. Ned visited him at four on Thursday to sound him out; Pellingham had his hired boy, Lonnie Pruitt, follow Ned that night. Lonnie heard the shots, saw a woman in a pale fur come out of the alley, and fished the pistol she dropped out of the ash can. Pellingham now holds the gun in a hatbox in his penthouse and Lonnie's story in his pocket, and has used both to make Corinne promise him the crane. He has never fired a gun in his life.

Lonnie Pruitt, 21, the gunsel, a peach-picker's son from Lodi who carries two .32 pocket pistols he has never fired at a person. He is nervous because he is the only witness to a murder, he is carrying a story nobody would believe from him, and both of his own guns are the same calibre as the one that killed Ned. He wants to go home.

Mick Larrabee, 50, who runs Pier 32 and a hauling company with night contracts on Treasure Island. Carlton Marsh owed him $6,000 and, to buy time, told him in his cups that he was 'bringing home a bird full of ice'. Larrabee believes the crane is stuffed with diamonds. His man inside Homicide is Dolan's own sergeant, Wally Kerrigan.
Corinne Marsh, who knows from Carlton's last letter exactly what is in the base and whose it is.
controlFile.theLieutenant: Lieutenant Frank Dolan, 47, Homicide, is honest, grieving and wrong. Ned Corrigan trained him as a young detective and Dolan loved him. He suspects the agency because Ned and Cass Delaney carried $5,000 key-man insurance policies on each other, because the elevator man heard Cass and Ned shouting at each other that afternoon about taking the job, because Ned's gun was holstered (he knew his killer), and because two of the agency's people carry .32s. He has Ned's notebook, taken from the body, and is withholding it because the last page reads 'C. says drop it'. He is not bent, does not want to frame anyone, and will change his mind for evidence, but he will arrest Cass at midnight on Armistice Day if he has nothing better. His sergeant, Wally Kerrigan, is Larrabee's man, and that betrayal will hurt him more than anything the party does.
redHerrings: The client: three names, a Viennese accent, a silver fox collar of her own, a real name beginning with M (Ned's blotter reads 'M. 11 Tallow'), and a reason to want Ned to keep quiet. Cleared by the Western Union time-stamp and, in detail, by the fur: her collar is an old, worn, moth-nibbled pelt; the hairs on Ned's sleeve are from a new ranch-bred stole.

Lonnie Pruitt: at the scene, carries two .32s, runs whenever he sees the party. Cleared by the casings (Colt ejector marks; his guns are Spanish-made Rubys with a different breech face) and by his account when he finally gives it.
Ambrose Pellingham: wants the crane more than anyone, stays on Nob Hill like the killer, and is concealing evidence. He was in his penthouse with a buyer from Gump's until half past midnight.
Mick Larrabee: owed money, violent, a waterfront boss. He was at the Anchor Grill on the Embarcadero all evening in front of forty longshoremen.
Cass Delaney and the agency: insurance, the argument, the .32s. The argument was Cass telling Ned the client was lying; she was right.
clues: A1: Ned's holstered revolver, no defensive wounds, and a cigarette lighter in his hand: he met someone he did not fear. (bc-scenario-001)
A2: Dot Farrell heard half of Ned's 6:15 telephone call: 'Then eleven, the back of the warehouse. You'll see it's the decent thing.' (bc-scenario-001)
A3: The impression on Ned's desk blotter: 'M. 11 Tallow'. M is for Marsh, though it looks like it could be for the client. (bc-scenario-001)
A4: The city directory and the warehouse door: the loading door where Ned died belongs to Marsh Pacific Trading, Carlton Marsh deceased, Corinne Marsh proprietor. (bc-scenario-001)
B1: The Sir Francis Drake's register: 'Mrs. Helen Strand' was registered as 'Miss Marta Lind' and checked out at seven on Friday morning. (bc-scenario-001)
B2: The client's two hundred dollars came in a Bank of America foreign exchange wrapper, changed from Portuguese escudos. (bc-scenario-001)
B3: Anton Weisz or anyone who speaks German hears a Viennese accent; the coat label reads 'Lindner, Wien'. (bc-scenario-001)
B4: Rose Fong at the telephone exchange, or the Drake's bell captain: 'Miss Lind' moved to the Hotel Grant on Bush Street, a residential hotel by the week. (bc-scenario-001)
C1: The client's carbon of a Marsh Pacific bill of lading: one crate, 'objet d'art, lacquer', Serra da Estrela, Lisbon via Panama. (bc-scenario-001)
C2: The Mark Hopkins doorman: Ned went up to the penthouse at four; Mr. Pellingham's 'young man' left after him and came back after midnight in a hurry. (bc-scenario-001)
C3: The Chronicle's shipping column and the Marine Exchange: Serra da Estrela due Monday 7 November, Pier 32. (bc-scenario-001)
G1: Silver fox guard hairs on Ned's right sleeve and lapel, new ranch-bred pelt. (bc-scenario-001, Forensics on the body)
G2: The Friday society page: Mrs. Carlton Marsh 'in mourning grey and silver fox' at the Community Chest ball at the Fairmont. (bc-scenario-001)
G3: Rose Fong, walking home from the exchange at 11:08, saw a woman in a pale fur hurrying up Kearny toward California Street with one hand inside her coat. (bc-scenario-001)

G4: The California Street cable-car crews at the car barn at California and Hyde: a lady in grey and silver fox rode down from Mason Street at about 10:45 and back up from Kearny at about 11:25, and tipped the conductor a silver dollar, which nobody does. (bc-scenario-001 or 003)

D1: Carlton Marsh's effects, carried home by the Serra da Estrela's purser: a carbon of his last letter to Corinne, naming the Ehrlichs and the bonds: 'The bird is theirs, Viv, and what's in her belly is theirs. I'm only the porter.' (bc-scenario-002)
D2: The Serra da Estrela's mate, Joaquim Lobo: Carlton told him over brandy that he was carrying 'a whole family's life in a wooden bird'. (bc-scenario-002)
D3: Magda Ehrlich's own account, once she is confronted with D1 or the names. (bc-scenario-002)
E1: The purser's inventory of Carlton's effects: no pistol. (bc-scenario-002)
E2: The same letter: 'I left the Colt in the bedside drawer for you. The house is too big with me away.' (bc-scenario-002)

E3: The pistol register at the Hall of Justice: a Colt .32 automatic, serial 482117, sold to Carlton J. Marsh in 1931. Corinne told the party, and Dolan, that Carlton took it to Lisbon and it was lost with his things. (bc-scenario-002)

H1: The Western Union office on Market Street: the client's cable to Dr. O. Ehrlich in Lisbon, time-stamped 11:02 pm on Thursday 3 November, seventeen blocks from Tallow Alley. It clears her. (bc-scenario-002)

F1: Kenji Okada, lacquer restorer in Japantown: the base has been opened twice, once in Lisbon with a craftsman's care, and again within the last week, crudely, with a heated knife; the new shellac is still soft. (bc-scenario-003)

F2: Concepción Ruiz, Corinne's housekeeper: on Wednesday night Mrs. Marsh sent her to bed early and melted something on the kitchen stove; there is shellac on a burnt newspaper in the ash bin. (bc-scenario-003)
F3: The Matson office on Market Street: Mrs. Marsh bought a one-way first-class passage to Honolulu on Thursday morning, before the auction. (bc-scenario-003)
F4: Harlan Fitch, a bond dealer on Montgomery Street: a widow in grey asked him on Wednesday afternoon how a person might sell $38,000 of bearer Treasuries 'without a fuss'. (bc-scenario-003)
F5: Larrabee's men, when caught on Treasure Island: the base was empty when they cracked it with a tire iron. (bc-scenario-003)

F7: Mr. Gilchrist: Mrs. Marsh insisted on an evening sale on the house's own insurance terms (lots insured at their 0,000 reserve while on the premises) and asked about the insurance twice. (bc-scenario-003)

P1: A brown Roos Bros. fedora with L.P. inked inside the band, picked up at the mouth of Tallow Alley at 11:15 by Rose Fong's uncle, the printer on Jackson Street. It is Lonnie's. (bc-scenario-003; also available from bc-scenario-001 to anyone who asks the printer)
P2: Lonnie Pruitt, in the dark at the auction: 'I didn't shoot nobody. I swear to God. I only picked it up.' (bc-scenario-003)
P3: Pellingham to Corinne at the viewing, overheard: 'A sale, madam, was not our understanding. Remember what I hold of your husband's.' (bc-scenario-003)

G5: The Fairmont's cloakroom attendant, Annie Rourke, kept a pair of dove-grey French kid evening gloves she found in the ladies' lounge wastebasket at 11:40 on Thursday night; the right forefinger is stippled with powder burns and there is a brown spot on the cuff. (bc-scenario-003)
G6: Ned's notebook, which Dolan will share once he trusts the party: last page, 'V.M. says Carlton never told her a thing. Liar.' and 'C. says drop it'. (bc-scenario-003)
G7: Lonnie Pruitt's eyewitness account: the woman in the pale fur, the ash can, the pistol. (bc-scenario-004)
G8: The pistol itself, in Pellingham's hatbox: Colt .32, serial 482117. Dr. Lindqvist's comparison microscope matches its ejector marks to the two casings from Tallow Alley. (bc-scenario-004)
controlFile.underTheLacquer: Everybody has a story. Pellingham: 'Hinoki cypress and three hundred years, sir. The lacquer is the treasure.' (He is right.) Larrabee: 'Ice. Carlton said a bird full of ice.' (Carlton lied to him.) Sergeant Kerrigan: 'Spanish gold. Half the Republic's gold went out through Lisbon.' (It did not.) Lonnie: 'Mr. P says there's a saint's finger in it.' (Pellingham told him so to make him careful.) Corinne, in turn: 'Nothing, it was a present for me'; then 'Carlton's savings, which are mine'; then 'Some papers, I don't know what'. Dolan: 'It's a wooden bird, and a man's dead over it.' Magda says nothing, because she knows.
controlFile.theMoralChoice: In the penthouse on the last night the party can have justice, the Ehrlichs' money, and the crane, but not easily all three. Pellingham will hand over the pistol and Lonnie (who is in his employ and in his debt) only in exchange for the crane. Without the pistol, the case against Corinne rests on the gloves, the cable car, the fur and the pistol-register lie: enough for Dolan to arrest her, perhaps not enough for a jury against a Nob Hill lawyer. When Corinne is exposed the bonds become evidence of motive, and Dolan by the book will impound them; the Ehrlichs would miss the 18 November deadline and lose their visas. Corinne will offer the party half the bonds, $19,000, to let her reach the boat. Larrabee wants his $6,000 from somewhere. Magda, who has her own voice in this, will say that her father would trade a hundred cranes for one more day of his family's safety, but that the crane was her mother's favourite thing, and that she wants the person who killed Mr. Corrigan to pay. Dolan can be persuaded to let the bonds go to the family (Persuasion DC 15, with advantage if the party has shown him the evening paper about the pogrom, or has been straight with him all week) at the cost of his own rules. There is no right answer. There are several honest ones.
controlFile.outcomes: If Corinne is arrested with good evidence, she is tried in the spring and the jury believes the cable-car crew and the cloakroom girl. If the evidence is thin, her lawyer gets her off, and she is ruined anyway. If she reaches the ship, she lands in Honolulu with whatever she still has, and the party knows, and Dolan knows they let her. If the bonds reach Magda by the 18th, the Ehrlichs sail from Lisbon in December and Dr. Ehrlich writes to the agency from New York in January. If not, the GM should not make it an atrocity on the table: a cable in December says the family has been given a three-month extension by a decent consul, and the players carry the weight of how close it was. Cass Delaney keeps the agency or loses it according to what Dolan believes at the end. Ned is buried at Holy Cross in Colma on Monday 14 November, and everyone who matters comes.
